name: Calories Don't Count diet

lead: Calories Don't Count is a diet popularised by the 1961 book of the same name by New York obstetrician-gynecologist Herman Taller. It promoted meals high in fat and low in carbohydrate, plus safflower oil capsules, with the promise of losing weight without counting calories.

The appeal for people seeking a leaner look was permission to eat fat-rich food freely. The book sold more than two million copies, but physicians criticised it and Taller was later convicted of mail fraud. It is an early ancestor of later low-carbohydrate diets.

paras: The plan as described emphasised high-fat foods, restricted carbohydrate, and daily safflower oil capsules, which Taller said stimulated the pituitary to burn fat. It was followed at home from the book.

Medical experts of the time described the diet as dangerous and FDA Commissioner George Larrick said calories do count. Early editions' safflower capsule claims led to legal action. Anyone considering a major diet change typically consults a clinician.

social.title: "Why Calories Don't Count: How We Got the Science of Weight Loss Wrong", Dr. Giles Yeo, Geneticist. #medicine #biology

chain: Believers expect fat loss without counting calories
angle.text: The diet was marketed as a way to get slim by changing food composition rather than restricting calories. Its core claims were disputed by physicians and regulators.

lead: Calories Don't Count is a weight-loss book published in 1961 by Herman Taller, a Romanian-born American obstetrician and gynecologist in New York [1]. It argued for a high-fat, low-carbohydrate diet with high-dose safflower oil capsules and held that carbohydrates, through pyruvic acid, block fat burning [1].

People used it to slim down without conscious calorie restriction. Medical experts widely criticised it, and the FDA alleged the book chiefly served to sell the capsules; Taller was convicted of mail fraud and conspiracy in 1967 [1]. It sold over two million copies and is cited by historians as an example of a fad diet [1].

The slogan has recurred. Medical journals responded in the 1960s with titles such as a 1963 American Journal of Medicine piece, and later authors have used the phrase for other arguments, such as geneticist Giles Yeo's talk on why calorie counts on food labels are imperfect [2][3][4][5].

paras: Taller's book proposed that safflower oil stimulates the pituitary gland to burn fat faster and that carbohydrate-derived pyruvic acid prevents fat burning [1]. It encouraged high-fat meals and restricted carbohydrate [1].

The FDA alleged the book existed mainly to promote safflower capsules in which Taller had an interest; Commissioner George P. Larrick called the capsules worthless. Simon & Schuster denied the allegations [1]. After trial and an appeal on jury instructions, Taller was convicted in 1967 of mail fraud and conspiracy and fined $7,000; later editions dropped the capsules [1].

Journals responded directly: the American Journal of Medicine published 'Calories Don't Count - If You Don't Use Them' in 1963, and Brazilian medical journals ran critiques in 1965 and 1966 [2][4][5]. Larrick's remark that calories do count became a standard rejoinder [1].
No studies found testing Taller's safflower-oil regimen. The 1960s journal articles are commentaries on the claims [2][4][5].
